FCAPS is the ISO Telecommunications Management Network (TMN) model and framework for network management. The acronym stands for the five functional areas required to manage a network effectively:
Fault Management: Detecting, isolating, logging, and resolving network hardware or software failures (e.g., handling SNMP traps, link-down alerts, and root-cause analysis).
Configuration Management: Tracking, modifying, and backing up network hardware and software configurations, as well as provisioning new devices and documenting network topology.
Accounting Management: Measuring and tracking network utilization metrics per user, department, or service—used for billing, chargebacks, and capacity planning.
Performance Management: Monitoring throughput, latency, packet loss, jitter, and bandwidth utilization to ensure the network meets Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
Security Management: Controlling access to network resources, enforcing security policies, managing firewalls/VPNs, and auditing logs for unauthorized activity or breaches.

No, that is actually the opposite of how SNMP traps work. SNMP traps are asynchronous, unsolicited notifications sent by the managed device (agent) to the SNMP manager when a significant event happens—without waiting for the manager to poll.
Traps vs. Polling (GET Requests)
Feature SNMP Polling (GET / GETNEXT / GETBULK) SNMP Traps (TRAP / INFORM)
Who initiates? The SNMP Manager asks the device. The Managed Device (Agent) pushes the alert.
Timing Periodic / on-demand (e.g., every 1–5 minutes). Event-driven / immediate (e.g., link down, fan failure, reboot).
Network overhead Predictable, steady traffic; can miss brief spikes between polls. Quiet during normal operation; bursts when events occur.
Delivery guarantee Manager waits for response (or retries). TRAP is unacknowledged (UDP); INFORM (SNMPv2c/v3) expects an acknowledgment.
Why Both Are Used Together
Polling gives you a continuous baseline and metrics over time (like CPU utilization or interface throughput) so you can spot gradual trends.
Traps give you near-instant alerts for state changes or faults between polling intervals (like a port going down or a power supply failing).
If you're setting up SNMP monitoring and traps aren't arriving—or you're deciding between traps and polling for a specific device—let me know what equipment or monitoring tool you're working with and I can help troubleshoot. (Signing in to a Google Account is also handy if you'd like to save this conversation and come back to your notes later.)
